title: This Canvas Is Filed as Abstract Expressionism. Its Own Patron Said He Belonged to No School at All.
standfirst: William Congdon built this Venice canal with a masonry knife nine years after he was among the first Americans into Bergen-Belsen, and Peggy Guggenheim, the collector who did most to get his work seen, insisted he fit no movement whatsoever. The label this picture now carries disagrees with her — and so, it turns out, does the title written on its own reverse.

sections.heading: A Knife, Never a Brush
sections.body: In 1954 Congdon set out his method in one line: "Use a knife – never a brush which only compromises. A knife constructs!" He worked paint on with masonry tools, palette knives, awls and spatulas, sometimes cutting straight through to the board, sometimes mixing in ash or gold dust before it set. That is not a stylistic flourish borrowed from the New York painters he admired. Congdon had volunteered as an ambulance driver on 20 April 1942, and the three years that followed took him through Syria, El Alamein, the Italian campaign at Monte Cassino, and into Germany — he was among the first Americans to enter Bergen-Belsen after its liberation. He spent part of the postwar period with the American Friends Service Committee, helping rebuild villages in Molise. By his own account, and by those who have written about him since, it was the search for a visual language equal to the camps, and to Hiroshima, that pushed him out of sculpture and into paint he could gouge rather than merely apply. The scarred, incised surface of a Venetian canal is the same hand.

sections.heading: Belongs to No School
sections.body: Peggy Guggenheim collected Congdon and said so in terms that still get quoted: "William Congdon is the only painter, after Turner, who has understood Venice, its mystery, its poetry, its passion." She went further, insisting that he "belongs to no group of painters. He stands apart. He belongs to no school." That has not stopped the label-makers. This picture is catalogued as Abstract Expressionism, and Congdon did call Braque, Klee, Pollock and Rothko his artistic fathers. But the art historian Paolo Biscottini has argued flatly that "Congdon was not a painter of abstract expressionism," preferring the term "figurative abstract." The distinction is not academic hair-splitting: in a true Pollock or Rothko the subject has gone. Here the Doge's Palace, the basin, the campanile are still legible under the knife marks, fighting the paint rather than dissolved by it. Guggenheim's Venice itself owns two of his other canvases from these years, Venice #1 and Piazza San Marco #15 — proof she put her own money behind the claim that he was not quite one of the group he is filed with.

sections.heading: A Gift to the Man Who Went With Him
sections.body: Congdon's American reputation came first. He moved to the Bowery in February 1948, was introduced to the dealer Betty Parsons through a frame-maker named Leo Robinson, and had his first solo show in May 1949. By 1951 Time magazine had run a long piece on him and the Whitney had given him a show — he was, briefly, one of the most written-about painters in New York. In 1950 he returned to Italy accompanied by Jim Ede, the Cambridge curator and collector who would later found Kettle's Yard, and the two of them painted their way through Venice and Rome on a trip that did more than anything else to establish Congdon's reputation there. He made this canal view in October 1952, on hardboard, at 840 by 1242 millimetres. The following year he gave it outright to Ede. That is the whole reason a major Congdon from his most celebrated decade hangs in a university house in England rather than a museum sale room: it was never sold at all.

sections.heading: Painted, Probably, From the Wrong Island
sections.body: The title under which this picture travels, Venice from the Giudecca, may simply be wrong. Congdon inscribed a generic title, Canal, Venice, on the reverse himself, leaving the more specific name to accumulate elsewhere, and Kettle's Yard's own cataloguing now states that the actual vantage point was more likely San Giorgio Maggiore, a different island with a different church, looking back across the same basin. Nobody has definitively settled it. That the error exists at all fits everything else known about how Congdon worked: he rarely painted in front of a subject, preferring, as one reviewer of a 2019 Cambridge retrospective put it, to use his work "to express what he felt in a place – not necessarily what he saw." A painter assembling a view from memory and feeling, back in a studio, is exactly the painter whose own label for it might drift half a mile across the water.

sections.heading: Fifty-Six Years, to the Day
sections.body: In 1959, after a trip to Cambodia, Congdon converted to Catholicism at Pro Civitate Christiana in Assisi, and the American market that had made him more or less dropped him for it; one retrospective of his Venice work notes that he was so little seen in the city that had made his name that the first major Congdon retrospective actually held in Venice did not happen until 2012, at Ca' Foscari, fourteen years after he died. From 1979 he lived as artist-in-residence beside a Benedictine monastery at Cascinazza, near Milan, and kept painting almost to the end. He had been born in Providence, Rhode Island, on the night the Titanic went down — 15 April 1912. He died in Milan on 15 April 1998: his eighty-sixth birthday, to the day.
